newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Transit fraud threatens Europe's TIR lorry system.
newsitem.headline: Transit fraud threatens Europe's TIR lorry system.

text.p: Europe's "TIR" lorry transport system faces collapse because insurers are no longer prepared to pay for trucks that go missing en route with consignments ending up in the hands of smugglers, a U.N. expert said on Thursday.

A breakdown of the TIR system, which enables lorries to bypass customs until their final destination, could lead to reimposition of strict border controls -- and customs queues -- in the European Union, where transit fraud has accompanied a surge in cargo traffic by road since the abolition of internal borders.

Martin Magold of the U.N. Economic Commission for Europe (ECE), which promotes economic cooperation in Europe, said transit fraud in Europe worth hundreds of millions of dollars could bring the system down if controls were not tightened.
He said the system nearly collapsed when insurance associations in Germany -- a crossroads for goods manufactured in the east entering Western Europe -- pulled out on October 28.
After negotiations, they withdrew their denunciation of guarantees but the future remained in doubt. An ECE meeting in Geneva on December 2-3 will discuss ways to tighten controls.
"German insurers are faced with a sudden avalanche of claims. They fear they won't get their money back," Magold said.
"There are no borders within the EU and we need to make the system safer. If German insurers withdraw guarantees, there is no more insurance and the TIR system can no longer be used."
Sealed TIR lorries account for the bulk of cargo transport by land across Europe, carrying goods from Norway to Iran and from Portugal to Kazakhstan.
Under the TIR convention, which originated in 1960, lorries are sealed and bear blue TIR plates to speed up frontier and customs formalities and are waved through at borders.

But lorry contents are often tampered, sometimes with the complicity of the drivers who report losses as accidental. The freight forwarder is liable for the consignment and duty bills when goods are transported overland.
Magold said more than $100 million worth of claims against fraud came from Germany and another $100 million from Russia, where mafia has flourished since the 1991 Soviet collapse.

Cigarettes and alcohol used to be the smugglers' favourites until they were excluded from the TIR system last year. They have been replaced by subsidised EU goods such as meat and milk products as well as computers and electronics goods.
